title: Not beyond what you can bear
word: Not beyond what you can bear
hook: Allah burdens no soul beyond its capacity, our Lord, forgive us (2:286)
carry: not beyond what I can bear

segments.voice: Yesterday, a long verse about a debt, a scribe and witnesses. Your line was write it down. Did you write down something you owe? Day three hundred sixty-two, and the last day of al-Baqarah.

Al-Baqarah is two hundred eighty-six verses long. We've walked through it for almost a month: the cow, the Throne verse, no compulsion, a man asleep for a hundred years, a grain that becomes seven hundred, a debt written down. It holds laws, stories, warnings and arguments. And then, at the very end, it does something unexpected. It stops talking to people and turns into words people say back. The surah's last verse is a list of requests, and it opens with a promise about weight.
screen: `286 VERSES.` → `LAWS, STORIES, A DEBT.` → `THE END TURNS INTO A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, the verse opens: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The Arabic word for scope is wus'a, capacity, the room a thing has inside it. Every soul has a size, and the verse says what's asked of it fits inside. Then come the requests, each starting with our Lord. Don't take us to task if we forget or slip. Don't lay on us a burden like the one laid on those before us. Don't make us carry what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. There's a story behind it, in Sahih Muslim. When the verse just before, 2:284, came down, saying God will call people to account for what's in their hearts, whether they show it or hide it, the companions were frightened. They came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ on their knees and said this was more than they could carry. He told them to say instead: we hear and we obey. They said it, and then these last two verses came, the believers' answer and this list of requests. A related report in the same collection, from Ibn Abbas, says that after each request, God answered: I have done so. A second hadith, in Bukhari, says whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him. Scholars give different meanings for enough: enough protection, enough of a night prayer, or both. So the surah ends where some people end their day, in bed, saying these two verses. It doesn't promise that nothing will be heavy. It says the weight was measured to the one carrying it.
screen: `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE: WUS'A, CAPACITY` · `OUR LORD: A LIST OF REQUESTS` · `THE FRIGHTENED COMPANIONS` · `ENOUGH FOR THE NIGHT` · then, large: `ALLAH TASKETH NOT A SOUL BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: Tonight, if you'd like, read or recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah before you sleep, in Arabic or in a translation. For now, sit comfortably and let the bell start. Bring to mind one thing that feels heavy right now. Don't solve it. Just notice how big it is, and then notice that you are still here, holding it. On each out-breath, let the line be there: not beyond what I can bear. If you pray, you can add the verse's own words: our Lord, pardon us. The bell holds the time.
Not beyond what you can bear. God asks no soul more than its capacity, its wus'a, from the last verse of al-Baqarah. Today's word.
screen: `NOT BEYOND WHAT YOU CAN BEAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not beyond what I can bear. When something lands on you today, say the line once before you react, and remember the companions on their knees, and the answer that came. Day three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah (2:285–286) every night before sleeping, following a hadith that they suffice whoever reads them at night; the requests of 2:286 are also said often in personal supplication.

original.note: Arabic: God does not burden a soul except to its capacity (2:286).

trapdoor: what you thought: God won't give you more than you can handle.
what it means: what God asks of a soul fits within its capacity, and the verse turns at once into requests for pardon and mercy.
what a scholar hears: wus'a, capacity, a word about room and width; and a report in Sahih Muslim that 2:285–286 came down after 2:284 alarmed the companions.
